claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit unusually high mechanical strength at elevated temperatures.
Refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit thermoelastic stability at elevated temperatures.
Composition-dependent local lattice distortions raise the energy barriers for dislocation glide and climb.
Sluggish diffusion slows diffusion-controlled recovery processes at high temperatures.
The combination of lattice misfit and sluggish diffusion enhances high-temperature yield-strength retention.
The combination of lattice misfit and sluggish diffusion minimizes thermal softening during high-temperature service.
Adding a small amount of V to an NbMoTaW-type alloy will increase atomic-size mismatch and local lattice distortion.
Size and modulus mismatches among refractory elements generate a complex local energy landscape.
The local energy landscape produced by lattice distortion acts as robust dislocation-pinning sites.
Reduced atomic mobility limits dynamic recovery at high temperatures.
Sluggish diffusion impedes dynamic recrystallization and dislocation climb.
An alloy with augmented lattice distortion will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the baseline alloy.
An alloy with augmented lattice distortion will have a lower high-temperature creep rate than the baseline alloy.
An alloy with augmented lattice distortion will have a higher elastic modulus than the baseline alloy.
An alloy with augmented lattice distortion will have lower thermal expansion than the baseline alloy.
The magnitude of lattice distortion will correlate positively with high-temperature strength retention.
Between approximately 0.4Tm and 0.7Tm, thermally activated dislocation and creep mechanisms are active while diffusion remains sufficiently sluggish for lattice-distortion effects to persist.
The proposed comparison requires baseline and modified alloys to be tested at identical temperature, strain-rate, stress, and environmental conditions.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys that remain single phase without precipitation or phase separation during high-temperature exposure.
Failure to observe statistically significant mechanical or thermoelastic changes correlated with increased lattice distortion would falsify the hypothesis.
